newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ford says Korea, Japan main threat to European jobs.
newsitem.headline: Ford says Korea, Japan main threat to European jobs.

text.p: Unfair competition from Korea and Japan are are the biggest longterm threats to jobs in the European car industry, Ford of Europe said Tuesday.
Ford of Europe chairman Jacques Nasser said in an interview that talk of an imminent shakeout in the industry, following Ford of Britain and Renault job cutting action was premature.
Manufacturers will have to "resize" to more efficiently meet market needs, said Nasser, whose job of president, Ford Motor, includes responsibility for Ford's European operations.
Ford Europe will at least break even in 1997, after 1996's losses, Nasser said.
Nasser was in town to preside over the launch of Ford's new small coupe, the Puma, at the Geneva car show.
South Korean car makers, mainly Daewoo Motor Co and Hyundai Motor, have now achieved a market share of just under two percent in western Europe, up from almost nothing five years ago.
Some analysts have questioned the financial manouverings of Korean companies. Car companies complain that free access to Korean markets is denied to European companies.
The Japanese, after peaking at around 12.3 percent in 1991 have slipped to just over 10-1/2 percent, hammered back by the strength of the yen.

This persuaded Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Honda to start producing cars in a big way mainly in Britain, so-called transplant production. The Japanese made 715,000 cars in Europe last year, and this should rise to 1.2 million by 2000, according to London's Economist Intelligence Unit.

The weaker yen now offers more profitable exports from Japan, and with the opening of European markets in 2000 to unlimited car imports, the Japanese are quietly building up into a major threat again.
"I think the risks are there. If the Japanese and the Koreans are left unchecked i think it will create a situation in Europe where more jobs will be threatened," Nasser said.

General Motors Europe said earlier today that the 980 job cuts at Ford's Halewood plant in Britain and Renault's plan to close its factory at Vilvoorde, Belgium with the loss of 3,100 jobs signalled the start of a major and long delayed shakeout in Europe, hit by overcapacity and stagnant sales.

"I don't know whether its the start of a shakeout. European rationalisation has been going on for decades. I wouldn't overreact to it. But I would say however that we will see if not a rationalisation of capacity, certainly a resizing of capacity to more closely meet the demands that we see in Europe today."

"A couple of things are happening there. The market's relatively flat and we haven't seen very much growth, and secondly, the transplants and Japanese imports and the other Asian imports particularly from Korea, really are making it more difficult to keep employment levels in Europe where they have been in the past."

"So I do see a situation where if there's no market growth and the imports from Korea continue to come into Europe, then I think its simple arithmetic. Then you will have lower levels of employment, the lower level of employment will be translated into different actions by different companies."

"Employment is going to be the result of how efficient the manufacturers are, how effective European governments are in terms of economic monitoring and fiscal policies, and can we get fair trading practise from the Asian importers."
"Certainly the Koreans are a threat, and the Japanese with the current exchange rate for the yen, they fall into that category also."
Ford Europe lost $300 million in 1996, according to the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Will this be turned around in 1997?

"It's hard to say at this point. We will improve in 1997 and hope it will be fairly significant. We've got the actions in place to make sure that happens, but at this point I'm reluctant to forecast but we've got a reasonably good chance of coming out in the black."
The E.I.U. agrees, reckoning that Ford Europe will earn $400 million in 1997.
